steps.scene: You drive into a bank of fog. You can no longer make out the road much beyond the car in front.

question.prompt: When may you switch your fog lights on?

options.text: Whenever the weather turns bad
Once you can see less than 100 metres
Only after dark, whatever the visibility

question.explanation: Fog lights are for seriously reduced visibility — 100 metres or less. Below that they earn their glare.

steps.title: Off the moment it clears
steps.body: You MUST switch fog lights off when visibility improves. Be ready to use them again if it drops back below 100 metres.

question.prompt: The fog has lifted and your front fog lights are still on. What do you do?

options.text: Leave them on until you park
Leave them on if other drivers have theirs on
Switch them off while visibility stays good

question.explanation: Switch them off as soon as the weather improves, and switch them back on if visibility drops again.

a.label: Front fog lights
a.body: Help YOU see. Left on in clear weather they dazzle drivers coming the other way.

b.label: Rear fog lights
b.body: Help you BE seen. Left on in clear weather they look just like brake lights.

question.prompt: Why is leaving rear fog lights on after the fog clears dangerous?

options.text: They may be confused with your brake lights
They do the same job as the front ones, so it's harmless
The bulbs will fail sooner

question.explanation: A driver behind can't tell whether you're braking or have simply forgotten your rear fog lights.

steps.title: Poor, but not that poor
steps.body: Murky daylight that isn't seriously reduced calls for dipped headlights — seen by others, without the glare of fog lights.

question.prompt: Daytime visibility is poor but not seriously reduced. Which lights?

options.text: Front fog lights
Dipped headlights
None — it's still daylight

question.explanation: Dipped headlights make you visible without dazzling. Fog lights wait until visibility is seriously reduced.

steps.scene: Thick fog. A pair of tail lights swims into view ahead and you settle in behind them.

question.prompt: What's wrong with sitting close behind them?

options.text: They can't see hazards early either, so they may stop suddenly
Their fog lights will dazzle you
Nothing — following their lights keeps you on the road

question.explanation: The driver ahead sees hazards just as late as you do. Stay well back — the surface is likely wet too.

steps.title: Slow to what you can see
steps.body: In fog it is harder to judge what's ahead. Drive at a speed you could stop in within the distance you can see to be clear.

question.prompt: Why reduce your speed in fog?

options.text: Concentrating hard makes up for the speed
It's harder to see what's ahead of you
Fog makes the engine work harder

question.explanation: You can only stop within what you can see. In fog that distance is short, so your speed has to be too.

steps.wrongBelief: Fog just means taking a bit more care — nothing else about the journey changes.

question.prompt: What else should change before you set off?

options.text: Allow more time, and clean your windows and lights
Nothing — just concentrate harder on the way
Set off earlier and drive at your normal speed

question.explanation: Fog journeys take longer. Clean glass and lights, allow the extra time, and ask if the trip is essential.

steps.repairNote: Allow more time, clean your windows and lights before setting off, and consider whether the journey is essential.
